name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
cards: Define deep vein thrombosis.
Clot formation in the deep veins, usually in the legs.
What share of all deep vein thromboses occur in the upper extremity?
Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis is how many times more common than upper extremity?
About ten times.
Most common causes of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis?
Pacemakers, implantable defibrillators and indwelling central venous catheters.
Pulmonary embolism rate: upper versus lower extremity thrombosis?
Up to 6% versus 15% to 30%.
Where does lower extremity deep vein thrombosis usually begin?
In the calf, then it moves proximally.
Most common proximal veins affected in the leg?
Femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh.
Most common distal veins affected in the leg?
Peroneal veins in the calf.
Which veins are affected during pregnancy?
Pelvic veins.
Age threshold listed as a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis?
Older than 60 years.
Which bowel diseases raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
How much does a prior deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism raise recurrence risk?
Several-fold higher, roughly 3 to 10 times.
Postpartum window of raised deep vein thrombosis risk?
The first 6 to 12 weeks.
Which leg symptom is most sensitive for deep vein thrombosis?
Swelling, at 97% sensitivity.
Sensitivity of leg pain and of leg warmth?
86% and 72%, respectively.
Classic calf complaint that persists and worsens over days?
A cramp or charley horse in the lower calf.
Define the Homan sign.
Calf pain on dorsiflexion of the foot.
How reliable is the Homan sign?
Neither sensitive nor specific.
Symptom pattern of an isolated distal deep vein thrombosis?
Symptoms confined to the calf.
Which mimic causes severe sudden calf discomfort?
Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.
Which mimic causes leg pain with redness, fever and chills?
Cellulitis.
Post-thrombotic syndrome appears how long after a deep vein thrombosis?
6 to 24 months.
Which mimic follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation?
Lymphedema.
Historic gold standard, replaced by duplex ultrasound?
Contrast ascending venography.
Fatal pulmonary embolism rate, untreated deep vein thrombosis without embolism?
Under 1%.
Fatal rate, untreated symptomatic nonmassive pulmonary embolism?
Fatal rate, untreated symptomatic massive pulmonary embolism?
About 9%.
Mainstay of deep vein thrombosis treatment?
Anticoagulation.
Classic anticoagulation strategy for deep vein thrombosis?
Heparin, then bridge to warfarin.
Which drug class is dabigatran?
Direct thrombin inhibitor.
Which drug class are rivaroxaban and apixaban?
Direct factor Xa inhibitors.
Which drugs follow 5 days of parenteral therapy?
Dabigatran or edoxaban.
Contraindications to anticoagulation?
Active bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma, severe bleeding disorders.
Duration when a major transient risk factor provoked the clot?
3 months.
Duration when a minor transient risk factor provoked the clot?
3 to 6 months.
Duration for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism?
Indefinite.
Which patients may be treated as outpatients?
Stable, low bleeding risk, normal kidneys, reliable follow-up.
Warfarin overlap with heparin lasts until when?
International normalized ratio above 2 for at least 24 hours.
Reversal agent for heparin?
Protamine sulfate.
Reversal agent for dabigatran?
Idarucizumab.
Reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban?
Andexanet alfa.
Only indication for an inferior vena cava filter?
Acute proximal leg thrombosis with bleeding or anticoagulant contraindication.
Which thrombolytic drug treats large proximal thrombosis?
Tissue plasminogen activator.
Which device prevents thrombosis in immobilized hospital patients?
Intermittent pneumatic compression.
Most feared complication of deep vein thrombosis?
Pulmonary embolism.

name: Virchow Triad & Wells Criteria
cards: Name the three parts of the Virchow triad.
Venous stasis, hypercoagulable state, endothelial trauma.
Which Virchow component means altered blood flow?
Venous stasis.
Which Virchow component means inherited or acquired clotting tendency?
Hypercoagulable state.
Which Virchow component means injury to the vessel wall?
Endothelial trauma.
Prolonged sitting and postoperative inactivity fit which Virchow component?
Venous stasis.
How much does immobilization raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
About 20 times.
Venous insufficiency and heart failure fit which Virchow component?
Venous stasis.
Factor V Leiden fits which Virchow component?
Hypercoagulable state.
Inherited defects listed under the hypercoagulable component?
Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency.
Cancer and pregnancy fit which Virchow component?
Hypercoagulable state.
Estrogen exposures listed under the hypercoagulable component?
Oral contraceptives and postmenopausal estrogen replacement.
What makes oral contraceptive risk even higher?
Tobacco smoking or obesity.
Trauma and burns fit which Virchow component?
Endothelial trauma.
Surgeries carrying the greatest deep vein thrombosis risk?
Knee replacement, hip replacement and hip fracture surgery.
Which drug use injures lower extremity veins?
Intravenous drug use.
In what settings is the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis used?
Outpatient and emergency department.
In which setting is the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis NOT used?
Inpatient (hospitalized) patients.
What does the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis estimate?
Pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis.
How many points is each positive Wells item usually worth?
One point.
Which Wells item subtracts points, and how many?
Alternative diagnosis as likely as thrombosis: minus two.
Wells cancer item: treatment or palliation within what time?
Within 6 months.
Wells item: bedridden for longer than what?
More than 3 days.
Wells item: major surgery within what time?
Within 12 weeks.
Wells calf swelling item: larger than the other leg by what?
More than 3 centimeters.
Where is Wells calf circumference measured?
10 centimeters below the tibial tuberosity.
Which superficial veins score in the Wells criteria?
Collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins.
Wells swelling item covering the whole limb?
Entire leg swollen.
Which tenderness scores in the Wells criteria?
Localized along the deep venous system.
Which edema scores in the Wells criteria?
Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
Which limb items score under Wells paralysis or immobilization?
Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilization of the leg.
Does a previously documented deep vein thrombosis score in Wells?
Yes, one point.
Does long travel score as Wells immobilization?
No; only bedridden, surgery or cast counts.
Is a positive Homan sign a Wells item?
No.
Do pregnancy and estrogen therapy score in Wells?
No; they are not Wells items.
Wells category for a score of zero or less?
Low likelihood.
Wells category for a score of 1 to 2?
Moderate likelihood.
Wells category for a score of 3 or greater?
High likelihood.
Which Wells criteria set is the most widely validated?
The Wells 2003 set.
High Wells score: is a D-dimer required before ultrasound?
No; it is optional ("if taken").
First test for a low Wells score?
D-dimer.
Low Wells score, positive D-dimer, negative thigh ultrasound: next?
Stop; the work-up ends.
Which test follows a high Wells score?
Ultrasound, skipping the D-dimer.
What does an elevated D-dimer imply?
Increased fibrinolysis.
How does the D-dimer perform diagnostically?
Sensitive but not specific.
Best use of the D-dimer for deep vein thrombosis?
Rule-out test.
Low Wells score with a negative D-dimer means what?
Stop; deep vein thrombosis is ruled out.
Low Wells score with a positive D-dimer means what?
Order an ultrasound.
Does a positive D-dimer confirm deep vein thrombosis?
No; it shows fibrinolysis somewhere.
Negative ultrasound with high Wells score: repeat ultrasound when?
In 1 week.
Other options after a negative thigh ultrasound with high risk?
Lower leg ultrasound or phlebography.

name: Chronic Venous Insufficiency & Varicose Veins
cards: Spectrum of chronic venous disease from mild to severe?
Telangiectasias, varicose veins, chronic venous insufficiency.
Another name for chronic venous insufficiency?
Postthrombotic syndrome.
What underlies chronic venous disease?
Venous hypertension.
Causes of venous hypertension?
Poor muscle pump, incompetent valves, thrombosis, nonthrombotic obstruction.
What relieves chronic venous disease symptoms?
Limb elevation and walking.
Cause of brown or blue-gray skin discoloration?
Hemosiderin deposits.
Signs marking advanced chronic venous insufficiency?
Edema, skin changes, venous ulceration.
Define lipodermatosclerosis.
Skin and fat scarring in the lower legs.
Define primary chronic venous insufficiency.
Intrinsic vein wall or valve abnormality causing reflux.
Define secondary chronic venous insufficiency.
Obstruction or valve incompetence after a prior deep vein thrombosis.
Most common cause of chronic venous insufficiency?
Prior deep vein thrombosis.
Share of patients with no known deep vein thrombosis history?
Another common cause besides prior thrombosis?
Progressive superficial venous reflux.
What happens to valve leaflets in postthrombotic syndrome?
They become thickened and scarred.
Primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency?
Progressive pitting edema of the lower leg.
Describe the stasis dermatitis rash.
Eczematous with erythema, scaling, weeping and crusting.
Usual location of a venous ulcer?
Above the ankle, medial or anterior.
How does chronic venous insufficiency cellulitis appear?
Blanching erythema, with or without pain.
Which diseases cause bilateral leg edema mimicking venous insufficiency?
Heart failure, chronic kidney disease, decompensated liver disease.
Which drug classes cause leg edema?
Calcium channel blockers, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazolidinediones.
Unilateral swelling with absent varicosities suggests which condition?
Lymphedema.
Bilateral symmetric edema just above ankles in women?
Lipedema.
Test assessing venous patency and valve competence?
Venous duplex ultrasound.
Which test precedes compression for a leg wound?
Ankle-brachial index.
Why is the ankle-brachial index checked before compression?
Compression is contraindicated in peripheral artery disease.
Gold standard for chronic venous disease, rarely needed?
Catheter-based venography.
Initial management of chronic venous insufficiency?
Skin care, leg elevation, exercise, compression.
How high should legs be elevated?
Above heart level.
Standard treatment for chronic venous insufficiency?
Compression therapy.
Where is graduated compression pressure greatest?
At the ankle.
Which antibiotics treat cellulitis in chronic venous insufficiency?
Cephalexin or clindamycin.
What must happen before a venous ulcer will heal?
Edema controlled and compression applied.
Which oral drug may speed ulcer healing?
Aspirin.
Which drugs treat inflamed stasis dermatitis?
Mid-potency topical corticosteroids.
Downside of valvuloplasty?
High postoperative rate of deep vein thrombosis.
Which findings prompt vascular specialist referral?
Arterial insufficiency, nonhealing or recurrent ulcers, significant saphenous reflux.
What combination produces varicose veins?
Venous reflux plus venous hypertension.
Most commonly involved varicose vein?
The great saphenous vein.
Most common predisposing factor for varicose veins?
Family history.
Activities that raise venous pressure and cause varicose veins?
Prolonged standing and heavy lifting.
Most common varicose vein symptom?
Dull, achy heaviness brought on by standing.
Long-standing varicose veins can progress to what?
Chronic venous insufficiency.
Varicose vein diagnosis is mainly what?
Clinical, with the leg dependent.
Conservative therapy for isolated varicose veins?
Elevation, exercise and compression.
Define sclerotherapy.
Injecting an agent to fibrose and obliterate veins.
Surgical options for varicose vein reflux?
Vein stripping, laser or radiofrequency catheter.

name: Thrombophlebitis & Arteriovenous Fistula
cards: Define superficial phlebitis.
Inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus.
Define superficial thrombophlebitis.
Phlebitis with thrombus.
Most common cause of lower extremity thrombophlebitis?
Varicose veins.
Most common cause of upper extremity thrombophlebitis?
Recent intravenous catheter use.
Which catheter is most often responsible?
Peripherally inserted central catheter.
Hormonal risk factors for thrombophlebitis?
Pregnancy or estrogen therapy.
Which lower extremity history also raises thrombophlebitis risk?
Superficial vein thrombosis without varicose veins.
Findings along a phlebitic vein?
Tenderness, pain, induration and erythema.
Classic palpable finding in thrombophlebitis?
An indurated cord along a superficial vein.
Findings suggesting septic thrombophlebitis?
High fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage.
Which erythema pattern suggests septic thrombophlebitis?
Erythema extending well beyond the vein margin.
Septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without what history?
Venous cannulation.
Confirmatory test for thrombophlebitis?
Venous duplex ultrasound.
Duplex finding in thrombophlebitis?
Noncompressible vein with clot and thick wall.
Ultrasound wall thickening alone means what?
Phlebitis.
Ultrasound wall thickening with clot means what?
Thrombophlebitis.
How often does thrombophlebitis cause serious complications?
Rarely.
How often does superficial thrombophlebitis embolize?
Rarely.
Typical thrombophlebitis treatment?
Warm compresses, compression, elevation and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Which nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are examples for thrombophlebitis?
Ibuprofen and diclofenac.
When may anticoagulation be started?
Extensive clot burden or intermediate or higher thrombosis risk.
Anticoagulants named for thrombophlebitis?
Unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin, fondaparinux.
When should thrombophlebitis be re-examined?
Within 7 to 10 days.
What follows persistent or worsening signs?
Repeat duplex ultrasound.
Define an arteriovenous fistula.
Abnormal connection between an artery and a vein.
What does an arteriovenous fistula bypass?
The capillary bed.
Where are upper extremity fistulas most often created?
For hemodialysis vascular access.
Most common cause of lower extremity fistulas?
Iatrogenic, from groin vascular access.
Preferred sites for a created hemodialysis fistula?
Upper arm or forearm.
What does a healthy fistula do with arm elevation?
Collapses completely.
Findings in a healthy dialysis fistula?
Diffuse thrill and soft bruit.
Timing of the bruit in a healthy fistula?
Both systolic and diastolic.
Which vessels does an iatrogenic fistula usually affect?
Femoral vessels.
What should follow a groin puncture?
Complete leg vascular exam comparing pulses with baseline.
Test confirming a suspected iatrogenic fistula?
Duplex ultrasound.
How is an arteriovenous fistula usually diagnosed?
Physical examination.
Complications to watch for with a fistula?
Infection, venous insufficiency, heart failure, ischemia.
Define the Nicoladoni-Branham sign.
Reflex slowing of heart rate on compressing a large fistula.
Imaging that confirms a fistula's location and size?
Computed tomography angiography or angiography.
Why is congenital fistula hard to treat?
Communications are numerous.
Conservative treatment of congenital fistula?
Elastic support hose.
Procedure that can remove a congenital fistula?
Embolization.
Treatment of an acquired fistula?
Surgery to remove it or shrink it.

name: Peripheral Artery Disease & Critical Limb Ischemia
cards: Define peripheral arterial disease.
Lack of blood flow to muscle relative to its metabolism, causing pain in those muscles.
Three segmental sites of lower-extremity arterial disease?
Aortoiliac, femoral-popliteal and tibial segments.
Age threshold for peripheral arterial disease without other risk factors?
Over 60 years old.
Age threshold for peripheral arterial disease with risk factors?
50 years old.
How much does smoking raise peripheral arterial disease risk?
Three times the risk of nonsmokers.
Which amino acid is linked to earlier-onset atherosclerosis?
Homocysteine.
What share of patients with peripheral arterial disease also have coronary artery disease?
Define intermittent claudication.
Muscle pain with activity, relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes.
Commonest site of claudication?
The calf.
Upper two-thirds calf claudication points to which artery?
Superficial femoral artery.
Lower third calf claudication points to which artery?
Popliteal artery.
Buttock and hip claudication points to which segment?
Aortoiliac disease.
Leriche syndrome triad?
Claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses, erectile dysfunction.
Skin and appendage findings in chronic limb ischemia?
Dry, thin, shiny skin with hair loss and brittle nails.
Define dependent rubor.
Deep red discoloration of the leg when it hangs down.
Buerger test, first step?
Elevate the leg to 45 degrees for one minute and look for pallor.
In darker skin, what replaces color in the Buerger test?
Temperature, skin texture and capillary refill.
Capillary refill threshold suggesting arterial disease?
Longer than 2 seconds.
Important simple bedside initial test for peripheral arterial disease?
Ankle-brachial index.
Ankle-brachial index band for claudication?
Ankle-brachial index band for rest pain and tissue loss?
What does an ankle-brachial index above 1.3 mean?
Calcified, noncompressible arteries, for example in diabetes.
Mainstay initial imaging when arterial stenosis is suspected?
Duplex ultrasound.
Gold standard test for peripheral arterial disease?
Conventional angiography.
Blood pressure goal in peripheral arterial disease with diabetes?
Below 130/80 mmHg.
Minimum exercise prescription for claudication?
30 to 45 minutes, three times a week, ideally supervised.
Antiplatelet that is also a vasodilator?
Cilostazol.
Treatment for hyperhomocysteinemia?
Folic acid with vitamins B12 and B6; it lowers homocysteine but has not cut heart attacks or strokes.
When is revascularization recommended for claudication?
Severe functional disability despite exercise or drug therapy.
Rest pain: where and when is it worst?
Forefoot and toes, on elevation or reclining, often at night.
What relieves ischemic rest pain?
Hanging the leg over the bed edge or walking around.
Typical arterial ulcer appearance?
Dry, punched out, painful, minimal bleeding at the toe tips.
Wet gangrene is what kind of problem?
A surgical emergency, with infection and risk of sepsis.
Principal use of a bypass graft?
Severe critical leg ischemia.

name: Acute Limb Ischemia, Atheroembolism & Carotid Disease
cards: Define acute limb ischemia.
Sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery; a vascular emergency.
Most common embolic source in acute limb ischemia?
The heart, in 80% to 90% of cases.
Two cardiac sources of limb emboli?
Atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after myocardial infarction.
The six P's of arterial assessment?
Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia.
Define poikilothermia.
Difficulty regulating body temperature.
Often the earliest neurologic sign of acute limb ischemia?
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
Rutherford category I?
Viable: no sensory loss or weakness, Doppler signals audible.
Rutherford category IIB prognosis?
Salvageable only with immediate revascularization.
Where is a category IIB limb evaluated and treated?
In a surgical suite.
Rutherford category III outcome?
Major amputation regardless of therapy.
First two actions in acute limb ischemia?
Immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin.
Time limit for catheter-directed thrombolysis?
Acute limb ischemia under 14 days' duration.
Thrombolytic drug named for acute limb ischemia?
Alteplase.
What embolizes in atheroembolism?
Fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.
Distal pulses in atheroembolism?
Usually remain palpable.
Hallmark digital finding of atheroembolism?
Blue toe syndrome.
Share of ischemic strokes caused by carotid disease?
Roughly 10 to 20%.
Commonest mechanism of carotid stroke?
Plaque rupture rather than occlusion with thrombosis.
Define transient ischemic attack.
Brief focal loss of neurologic function with no lasting damage; classically under 24 hours.
Define amaurosis fugax.
Transient monocular blindness, like a curtain descending.
Asymptomatic carotid disease definition window?
No stroke or transient ischemic attack in the last six months.
Most widely used initial carotid screening test?
Duplex ultrasonography.
Gold standard carotid imaging?
Digital subtraction angiography.
Screening asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis?
Recommended against by the preventive services task force.
Stenosis threshold for surgery in symptomatic carotid disease?
Over 70%.
Asymptomatic carotid surgery criteria?
Over 80% stenosis with life expectancy over 5 years.
Gold standard procedure for high-grade carotid stenosis?
Carotid endarterectomy.
Carotid stenting suits which patients?
Poor surgical candidates.

name: Aortic Aneurysm, Pseudoaneurysm & Dissection
cards: Define an aneurysm.
Localized dilation greater than 50% of normal vessel diameter.
Diameter at which the infrarenal aorta is aneurysmal?
Over 3 cm.
Saccular versus fusiform aneurysm?
Saccular is an outpouching of part of the wall; fusiform is circumferential.
Most common site of aortic aneurysm?
The abdominal aorta.
What share of abdominal aortic aneurysms are infrarenal?
Strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Ever smoking.
Which population has the highest aneurysm incidence?
Caucasian men.
Three protective factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Female sex, non-Caucasian race and diabetes.
Classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Severe abdominal or back pain, pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension.
Which finding is virtually diagnostic of rupture?
A pulsatile abdominal mass.
Define Grey Turner sign.
Flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
Initial screening study for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Abdominal ultrasound.
Best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study for an aneurysm?
Computed tomography angiography.
Surveillance for a 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysm?
Ultrasound every three years.
Surveillance for a 4.0 to 5.4 cm aneurysm?
Ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months.
Elective repair threshold in women?
5.0 cm or larger.
Rapid growth that mandates abdominal aneurysm repair?
0.5 cm in six months.
Vascular specialist referral size for aortic aneurysm?
4.5 cm or larger.
Aneurysmal pain at any size calls for what?
Urgent vascular referral.
Two methods of aneurysm repair?
Endovascular aneurysm repair or open graft replacement.
Arch thoracic aneurysm symptom and nerve?
Hoarseness from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Chest X-ray sign of thoracic aneurysm?
Widened mediastinal shadow.
Which thoracic aneurysms are always repaired?
All symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms.
Ascending thoracic aneurysm repair diameter?
Over 5.5 cm.
Descending thoracic aneurysm repair diameter?
Over 6.0 cm.
Commonest site of pseudoaneurysm?
Femoral artery after cardiac catheterization.
Pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm management?
Watch and wait; it may thrombose and regress.
Pseudoaneurysm procedure to seal the leak?
Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.
Pain of aortic dissection?
Sudden, severe, tearing or ripping chest pain.
Classic cause of medial degeneration in dissection?
Marfan syndrome.
Systolic target in acute aortic dissection?
100 to 120 mmHg.
Intravenous agents named for dissection, in order?
Esmolol first; nitroprusside added if pressure stays high.

name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy & Myocarditis
cards: Most common type of cardiomyopathy?
Dilated cardiomyopathy.
Define dilated cardiomyopathy.
Dilation and impaired contraction of one or both ventricles.
Shape of the heart after dilated remodeling?
Globular.
Which valve regurgitation appears first in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Mitral regurgitation.
Typical age range at presentation of dilated cardiomyopathy?
20 to 60 years.
Share of dilated cardiomyopathy that is familial?
Up to 35%.
Nutritional deficiency causing dilated cardiomyopathy?
Thiamine, vitamin B1.
Alcohol cardiomyopathy: can function recover?
Yes, if alcohol intake is reduced or stopped.
Timing of peripartum cardiomyopathy?
Last trimester to six months postpartum.
Heart sound in dilated cardiomyopathy?
S3 gallop.
Apical impulse in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Laterally displaced.
Define hepatojugular reflux.
Neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver.
What does a normal electrocardiogram do for dilated cardiomyopathy?
Almost rules it out.
Prominent echo feature of dilated cardiomyopathy?
Dilated, thin walls.
Define Kerley B lines.
1 to 2 cm horizontal lines meeting the pleura; pulmonary edema.
B-type natriuretic peptide level that makes heart failure unlikely?
Below 100 pg/mL.
Two drug classes every dilated cardiomyopathy patient gets?
A beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Defibrillator threshold in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Ejection fraction below 35% after maximum medical therapy.
Two indications for a left ventricular assist device?
Bridge to transplant or recovery, or destination therapy.
Sodium restriction in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Less than 2 grams per day.
Five-year mortality once symptoms emerge?
Primary indication for cardiac transplantation?
Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.
Define myocarditis.
Inflammatory disease of the myocardium.
Presumed commonest cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
Viral infection.
Who is particularly susceptible to myocarditis?
Young males.
Typical history before viral myocarditis?
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier.
Gold standard test for myocarditis?
Endomyocardial biopsy.
Which imaging shows the extent of myocardial inflammation?
Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.
Mainstay of myocarditis treatment?
Supportive care.
Fraction of mild myocarditis that later becomes dilated cardiomyopathy?
One third.

name: Hypertrophic, Restrictive & Stress Cardiomyopathy
cards: Define hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Left ventricular hypertrophy without a causative hemodynamic factor.
Region most often hypertrophied in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
The interventricular septum.
Inheritance of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Autosomal dominant.
Prevalence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
1 in 500 people.
Leading cause of sudden death in preadolescents and adolescents?
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Define systolic anterior motion.
The anterior mitral leaflet is pulled into the outflow tract.
Common presenting symptom of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Dyspnea.
Symptom marking high sudden-death risk that needs urgent work-up?
Syncope.
Define pulsus bisferiens.
An arterial pulse with a double systolic peak.
Outflow murmur location in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Left sternal border, 3rd or 4th intercostal space.
Does the obstructive murmur radiate to the carotids?
No; it radiates to the suprasternal notch.
Maneuvers that soften the obstructive murmur?
Squatting, passive leg raising and handgrip.
Maneuvers that increase the obstructive murmur?
Valsalva, standing and amyl nitrite.
Test of choice for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Echocardiography.
Wall thickness confirming hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
1.5 cm or more, unexplained.
Initial drug for outflow tract obstruction?
A beta blocker.
Drug classes to avoid in outflow obstruction?
Preload or afterload reducers and positive inotropes.
Antiarrhythmic that converts atrial fibrillation and flutter to sinus rhythm here?
Amiodarone.
Two septal reduction procedures?
Surgical myectomy and alcohol septal ablation.
Activity advice in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Regular mild to moderate exercise; strenuous or competitive sport by shared decision; stay hydrated.
Least common cardiomyopathy?
Restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in the United States?
Amyloidosis.
Define Kussmaul sign.
Paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration.
Electrocardiogram finding of cardiac amyloidosis?
Low QRS voltage.
Test that helps separate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis?
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; a thickened pericardium points to constriction.
Diuretic caution in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
Lowering preload can drop output from stiff ventricles.
Prognosis of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
The poorest of all heart muscle diseases.
Who gets Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Postmenopausal women, 90% of cases.
Trigger of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
A significant emotional or physical stressor.
Echo finding in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Mid and apical left ventricular hypokinesis or akinesis.
How is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy confirmed?
Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries.
Initial management of suspected Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Follow acute coronary syndrome protocols.
Cardiomyopathy strategy for adolescents?
Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and activity restriction if high risk.
Cardiomyopathy focus in the elderly?
Tailored therapy, cautious diuretics, symptom control and palliative discussions.

name: Supraventricular Rhythm Strips
cards: How much time does one small box on electrocardiogram paper represent?
0.04 seconds; the thin lines are 1 mm apart.
How much time does one large box on electrocardiogram paper represent?
0.20 seconds, made of five small boxes.
What is the normal PR interval?
0.12 to 0.20 seconds, three to five small boxes.
What is the normal QRS duration?
Narrow, under 0.12 seconds.
What rate and P waves define normal sinus rhythm?
Regular at 60 to 100, with a uniform P wave for every QRS.
How does the rate change with breathing in sinus arrhythmia?
Faster on inspiration and slower on expiration, with a normal P before every QRS.
What rate defines sinus bradycardia?
A regular sinus rhythm under 60 beats per minute.
What rate range defines sinus tachycardia?
A regular sinus rhythm above 100, up to 160 beats per minute.
What does the sick sinus syndrome strip usually show?
An irregular rhythm with a variable rate, from bradycardia to tachycardia up to 160.
In sinus node exit block, what happens to the impulse?
It is generated but cannot get out of the sinoatrial node.
In sinus arrest, what happens to the impulse?
It is not generated, leading to a junctional rhythm.
What alternates in tachy-brady syndrome?
A tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, with bradycardia or offset pauses.
What does the classic supraventricular tachycardia strip show?
Regular, above 160, with hidden P waves and a narrow QRS.
Which supraventricular tachycardia is irregularly irregular with no P waves?
Atrial fibrillation, usually at 110 to 160 with a narrow QRS.
How do focal atrial tachycardia P waves look?
One consistent abnormal shape, with one P wave for every QRS; regular rhythm.
How many P-wave shapes define multifocal atrial tachycardia?
At least three distinct P-wave shapes in the same lead; irregular rhythm.
What resting electrocardiogram findings show pre-excitation?
A short PR interval and a delta wave, recorded during normal sinus rhythm.
What is a delta wave?
A slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS complex, seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
What QRS does orthodromic accessory pathway reentry produce?
Narrow, with no delta wave and a retrograde P wave after the QRS.
What QRS does antidromic accessory pathway reentry produce?
Wide, with a delta wave; P waves are rarely seen.
Where does atrioventricular nodal reentry circulate?
Within the atrioventricular node itself; slow-fast is the most common type.
What are the P waves like in atrioventricular nodal reentry?
Hidden, in a regular narrow tachycardia usually at 140 to 180.
How does ventricular tachycardia look against atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White?
Ventricular tachycardia is regular at 150 to 200; the other is irregular, near 300.
What does atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White look like?
An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia, with some rates approaching 300.
What atrial rate and waves define atrial flutter?
Sawtooth flutter waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300.
Which conduction ratio is most common in atrial flutter?
2:1 block, where the node blocks one of every two flutter waves.
What does a premature atrial contraction look like?
An early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS.
What does a premature junctional contraction look like?
An early narrow QRS with a P wave inverted, buried in the QRS, or after it.
How do junctional P waves look in leads II, III and aVF?
Inverted, sitting before, buried in, or after the QRS.
Where does the P wave sit when a junctional beat starts at the top of the node?
Before the QRS with a short PR, because the atria beat first.
Where does the P wave sit when a junctional beat starts at the bottom of the node?
After the QRS, a retrograde P wave, because the ventricles beat first.
What is the usual rate of a junctional rhythm?
40 to 60 beats per minute, regular, with a narrow QRS.
What is bigeminy?
An ectopic beat every other beat; an ectopic every third beat is trigeminy.

name: Supraventricular Arrhythmia Management
cards: First-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, unstable sinus bradycardia?
Atropine, followed by a temporary pacemaker if it does not work.
Treatment for asymptomatic sinus bradycardia?
No treatment; most people with sinus bradycardia have no symptoms.
Treatment for chronic, symptomatic sinus bradycardia?
A permanent pacemaker.
Management of appropriate sinus tachycardia?
Treat the underlying cause, such as blood loss, hypoxia or hyperthyroidism.
Usual management of inappropriate sinus tachycardia?
Generally left untreated: beta blockers are poorly tolerated and the prognosis is benign.
Sick sinus syndrome when symptoms do not match the bradycardia?
Observation is appropriate once symptoms are shown not to correlate.
Sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic bradycardia?
A permanent pacemaker, after treating any underlying cause such as drugs.
Tachy-brady syndrome where the fast rhythm is ventricular tachycardia?
A permanent pacemaker with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.
First-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
A vagal maneuver, before any drug.
What follows a failed vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia?
Adenosine, which may be given twice and can reveal hidden P waves.
Treatment for unstable supraventricular tachycardia?
Immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage.
Why give adenosine when focal atrial tachycardia is suspected?
It is diagnostic: adenosine usually fails to terminate focal atrial tachycardia.
Acute drug for stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia?
An intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Which drug may chemically cardiovert focal atrial tachycardia?
Amiodarone; an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion instead.
Usually curative therapy for focal atrial tachycardia?
Catheter ablation of the focus, curative in about 90%.
Main management of multifocal atrial tachycardia?
Treat the underlying lung disease or heart failure.
First-line drug for orthodromic accessory pathway reentry?
Adenosine, after a vagal maneuver as for any stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Drug when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White?
Intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be repeated or used.
Which drug must never be used in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White?
Adenosine, because blocking the node leaves the pathway unopposed.
First-line chronic treatment of Wolff-Parkinson-White?
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway.
What almost always terminates atrioventricular nodal reentry?
Vagal maneuvers or adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is rarely required.
What is the pill-in-the-pocket option for nodal reentry?
A beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker taken when an episode starts.
Cure rate of catheter ablation for nodal reentry?
Over 95%, offered to a select subset of patients.
Educated patient ends a nodal reentry episode at home with a vagal maneuver: advice?
Urgent medical attention is usually not required.
Treatment for stable atrial flutter?
Rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Treatment for unstable atrial flutter or fibrillation?
Synchronized cardioversion.
Definitive management of atrial flutter?
Ablation, because flutter recurs often and resists rate control.
Anticoagulation needed before outpatient cardioversion of flutter or fibrillation?
21 days of anticoagulation.
Treatment for stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response?
Intravenous rate control.
Treatment for stable atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response?
Rate control by mouth, with anticoagulation guided by stroke risk.
Which CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) scores are low risk?
0 in a man or 1 in a woman; may not need anticoagulation.
What does the HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score estimate?
The risk of major bleeding in a patient on anticoagulation.
Preferred anticoagulants in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation?
Direct oral anticoagulants: dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban.
Warfarin target in atrial fibrillation?
An international normalized ratio of 2 to 3.
Treatment for asymptomatic premature atrial contractions?
None; counsel to avoid triggers and reassure about the benign rhythm.
Treatment for persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions?
A beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated.
When is catheter ablation used for premature atrial contractions?
When they are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation.
Treatment for asymptomatic, infrequent premature junctional contractions?
None; reassurance about the benign rhythm is often enough.
Junctional rhythm caused by high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome?
A permanent pacemaker.
Junctional rhythm in a healthy, asymptomatic athlete?
No treatment; it reflects increased vagal tone.

name: Supraventricular Arrhythmias: Causes & Who Gets Them
cards: In whom is sinus bradycardia a normal adaptive finding?
Well-conditioned, active people such as athletes, people asleep, and adults over 65.
Which three drugs cause sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome?
Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
Which endocrine disorder causes sinus bradycardia?
Hypothyroidism, alongside sinoatrial node ischemia, raised intracranial pressure and late infection.
Which endocrine disorder causes sinus tachycardia?
Hyperthyroidism, alongside hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism and infarction.
Which drug withdrawal causes sinus tachycardia?
Abrupt withdrawal of beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
Physiologic causes of sinus tachycardia?
Pain, anxiety and exercise, with no dizziness or nausea.
What defines inappropriate sinus tachycardia?
A fast sinus rate unexplained after secondary causes are excluded.
Which surgery-related injury causes sick sinus syndrome?
Injury to the sinoatrial node from cardiac surgery.
Most common fast rhythm in tachy-brady syndrome?
Atrial fibrillation.
In whom are supraventricular tachycardia symptoms more pronounced?
The elderly and people with underlying structural heart disease.
Above what rate does supraventricular tachycardia usually cause collapse?
Above 200, as in reentry or atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway.
Usual setting of focal atrial tachycardia?
Increased metabolic demand without heart disease; abrupt-onset palpitations.
Usual setting of multifocal atrial tachycardia?
Acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure.
Prognostic meaning of multifocal atrial tachycardia?
A poor prognostic sign.
What substrate does accessory pathway reentry need?
An accessory pathway, the bundle of Kent, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
How do patients with accessory pathway reentry most commonly present?
With palpitations.
Which type of accessory pathway reentry is more common?
Orthodromic: down the node and back up the pathway.
Who gets atrioventricular nodal reentry most?
Women far more than men, usually without heart disease.
Triggers for atrioventricular nodal reentry?
Exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics, or none at all.
Exam sign of atrioventricular nodal reentry?
The frog sign: visible neck pulsations with sudden palpitations.
Settings in which atrial flutter is common?
Atrial scarring after surgery, right-sided heart failure, pulmonary vascular disease.
Which atrial flutter carries a big risk of ventricular fibrillation?
1:1 flutter, which also causes extreme hemodynamic instability.
Listed risk factors for atrial fibrillation?
Hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history, obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol, older age.
When is atrial fibrillation a medical emergency?
With severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) or an acute infarction.
How long does paroxysmal atrial fibrillation last?
Under one week, usually ending without treatment.
What defines persistent atrial fibrillation?
Continuous for more than 7 days but less than one year.
When is atrial fibrillation called permanent?
When patient and clinician jointly stop trying to restore sinus rhythm.
In which lung disease are premature atrial contractions common?
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; also alcohol, stress and caffeine.
What may premature atrial contractions precede in heart disease?
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.
How many premature junctional contractions prompt a search for heart disease?
More than 10 per minute, or multifocal ones.
Listed causes of junctional rhythm?
Sick sinus syndrome, inferior infarction, recent cardiac surgery and digoxin toxicity.
Why might a healthy athlete have a junctional rhythm?
Increased vagal tone; it is generally well tolerated.

name: Heart Blocks & Bundle Branches
cards: PR interval in first-degree atrioventricular block?
Greater than 0.20 seconds and constant, with every P wave conducted.
PR interval pattern in Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block?
Lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops, then the cycle repeats.
PR interval pattern in Mobitz type II block?
Constant, 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, with random dropped QRS complexes.
PR interval in third-degree (complete) block?
Random: P waves and QRS complexes have no relationship.
Usual ventricular rate in complete heart block?
Usually below 40 per minute, set by the escape rhythm.
Where can P waves hide in complete heart block?
Buried in the QRS complex, the ST segment or the T wave.
Most common cause of first-degree atrioventricular block?
Age-related degenerative changes of the conduction system.
Most common cause of Mobitz type II block?
Acquired His-Purkinje disease: old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes.
Most common cause of complete heart block?
Acquired conduction system disease, especially degeneration of old age, hypertension and diabetes.
PR interval above which first-degree block usually causes symptoms?
Greater than 0.3 seconds: fatigue, shortness of breath, palpitations, chest pain.
Three drug classes that cause first-degree and Mobitz type I block?
Beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
Procedure named as a cause of Mobitz type I block?
Cardiac ablation, alongside vagal tone, nodal blocking drugs, Lyme carditis and nodal ischemia.
Infection named as a cause of every degree of atrioventricular block?
Lyme disease (Lyme carditis) appears on the cause list of every degree.
Parasitic infection named as a cause of complete heart block?
Chagas disease, the parasitic cause on the complete heart block list.
Endocarditis complication that causes complete heart block?
An associated abscess reaching the conduction tissue.
Infiltrative diseases named as causes of complete heart block?
Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis, listed with myocarditis as inflammatory and infiltrative causes.
Inflammatory diseases named as causes of Mobitz type II block?
Myocarditis and reactive arthritis are the inflammatory causes on the Mobitz type II list.
Usual presentation of Mobitz type I block?
Usually asymptomatic; symptomatic patients are considered for a permanent pacemaker.
Treatment of asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block?
No treatment unless symptoms are debilitating or heart failure symptoms appear.
Why is Mobitz type II block dangerous even without symptoms?
Unpredictable progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death.
Why is the escape rhythm of Mobitz type II weak and unreliable?
The block usually originates at the bundle of His.
Stokes-Adams attack?
A sudden faint or seizure from a rapid temporary drop in brain blood flow.
Emergent treatment of Mobitz type II or complete heart block?
Transcutaneous pacing, the emergent bridge before a permanent pacemaker.
Definitive treatment of Mobitz type II or complete heart block?
A permanent pacemaker, placed even when Mobitz type II causes no symptoms.
Three things that set symptom severity in complete heart block?
Ventricular escape rate, site of the escape rhythm and underlying heart disease.
Symptom of complete heart block tied to higher sudden-death risk?
Syncope, which is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
QRS width of a complete bundle branch block?
0.12 seconds or more; the 0.20 on one slide is wrong.
Two fascicles of the left bundle branch?
The anterior and the posterior fascicle, the sites of a fascicular block.
Lead V1 finding in left bundle branch block?
A dominant S wave in V1, the rS pattern.
Leads I, V5 and V6 in left bundle branch block?
Absent Q waves, with a monophasic R wave.
How is the left ventricle activated in left bundle branch block?
By electricity crossing the septum from the right side.
Leads V1 to V3 in right bundle branch block?
An rsR' pattern, the bunny ears, where the right-sided delay shows best.
Leads I and aVL in right bundle branch block?
A slurred S wave in leads I and aVL.
How does the septum depolarize in right bundle branch block?
Normally, through the intact left bundle branch.
Valve disease singled out as a cause of left bundle branch block?
Aortic stenosis, the valve disease singled out on the cause list.
Degenerative fibrotic conduction disease causing left bundle branch block?
Lenègre–Lev disease, a degenerative fibrotic disease of the conduction system.
Acute event causing right bundle branch block by raising right pressure?
Pulmonary embolism, by suddenly raising right ventricular pressure.
Chronic pulmonary vascular cause of right bundle branch block?
Pulmonary hypertension, a chronic cause of right bundle branch block.
Treatment of symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction?
A biventricular pacemaker; otherwise the block is usually left untreated.
How should a new left bundle branch block be regarded?
Always as a sign of pathology needing evaluation for heart disease.
Is a new right bundle branch block always pathological?
No: it may occur with no apparent underlying heart disease.
What do symptoms from either bundle branch block usually mean?
Severe underlying heart disease; they resemble a heart failure exacerbation.

name: Ectopics, Ventricular Tachycardia & Torsades
cards: Look of a premature ventricular contraction?
Early, wide and bizarre QRS complex with no P wave.
Look of a premature junctional contraction?
Early narrow QRS; P wave inverted, buried in the QRS or after it.
Look of a premature atrial contraction?
An early, abnormally shaped P wave arising in the atria.
Ventricular bigeminy?
Every other beat is an ectopic beat.
Ventricular trigeminy?
Every third beat is an ectopic beat.
Main causes to look for with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances, so check oxygenation, potassium and magnesium first.
Electrolyte disturbances that trigger premature ventricular contractions?
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia are the electrolyte triggers listed.
Substances that trigger premature ventricular contractions?
Alcohol, caffeine and stimulants, which low-risk patients are told to eliminate.
Where are premature ventricular contraction palpitations often felt?
In the neck, though most patients have no symptoms at all.
Premature ventricular contraction burden that marks high risk?
Over 15% of beats, or 15,000 a day.
Premature ventricular contraction burden that allows reassurance?
Under 1% of beats, or 1,000 a day, with a normal heart and no symptoms.
History that alone makes premature ventricular contractions high risk?
Prior syncope (also structural or conduction disease, or beat-induced cardiomyopathy).
First-line treatment for low-risk symptomatic premature ventricular contractions?
A beta blocker; catheter ablation if refractory or not tolerated.
Treatment of isolated beat-induced cardiomyopathy with heart failure symptoms?
Catheter ablation, the treatment for isolated beat-induced cardiomyopathy with heart failure.
First step for other high-risk premature ventricular contraction patients?
A beta blocker plus optimized treatment of the underlying heart disease.
How many consecutive premature ventricular contractions make ventricular tachycardia?
Three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions.
Rate range of ventricular tachycardia?
100 to 250 per minute, regular, with a wide QRS.
What makes ventricular tachycardia sustained?
Lasting 30 seconds or more, or causing collapse in under 30 seconds.
Monomorphic versus polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
Same QRS shape every beat versus a QRS shape that varies.
Usual setting of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia?
Existing heart disease: heart failure, cardiomyopathy or prior infarction.
Most common cause of polymorphic tachycardia with a normal QT?
Acute myocardial ischemia, followed by cardiomyopathy.
First-line drug for symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia?
A beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol.
Antiarrhythmics for non-sustained tachycardia when beta blocker and ablation fail?
Amiodarone, lidocaine or procainamide, tried when ablation is not an option.
Management of asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia?
Optimize treatment of the underlying cardiac comorbidities.
Is non-sustained ventricular tachycardia an implantable defibrillator indication?
Not by itself; some patients qualify for primary prevention.
Drugs for stable sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia?
Intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide for pharmacologic cardioversion.
When is procainamide avoided in stable wide-QRS tachycardia?
With a prolonged QT or heart failure.
Four signs of hemodynamic instability in ventricular tachycardia?
Chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath, hypotension.
Unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse?
Synchronized cardioversion; without a pulse it becomes defibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, even with a pulse?
Defibrillation, then urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.
Torsades de pointes?
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline.
Key risk factor for torsades de pointes?
A long QT interval, congenital or (most often) acquired.
Electrolyte causes of acquired QT prolongation?
Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia, alongside the many QT-prolonging drugs.
First treatment for torsades in a conscious patient?
Intravenous magnesium push, then more magnesium as an infusion.
Why avoid amiodarone and procainamide in torsades?
Both prolong the QT interval and can feed the torsades.
Why avoid beta blockers in drug-induced torsades?
Bradycardia lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.
Antiarrhythmic that can be used in torsades?
Intravenous lidocaine, though the evidence is limited.
Hemodynamically unstable torsades de pointes?
Defibrillation, an unsynchronized shock, for torsades with hemodynamic instability.

name: Arrest Rhythms & Defibrillators
cards: Sudden cardiac death: time window?
Unexpected natural cardiac death within one hour of collapse.
Four rhythms of cardiac arrest?
Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity and asystole.
Most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death?
Coronary artery disease, even without a prior myocardial infarction.
What does an implantable cardioverter defibrillator do?
Sensing electrodes detect fatal arrhythmias and the device delivers a shock.
What else can newer implantable defibrillators do?
Act as pacemakers as well as delivering shocks.
External option that detects and shocks fatal ventricular rhythms?
A wearable cardioverter defibrillator vest (LifeVest) worn on the body.
After unstable ventricular tachycardia is stabilized, most patients need?
An implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death.
Pulseless monomorphic ventricular tachycardia?
Defibrillation, then managed exactly like ventricular fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation on the monitor?
Uncoordinated activity only: rate 0, no P waves, PR or QRS.
Two shockable arrest rhythms?
Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are the two shockable rhythms.
Two unshockable arrest rhythms?
Asystole and pulseless electrical activity: start compressions, never shock.
First treatment for ventricular fibrillation?
Defibrillate as soon as possible, an unsynchronized shock.
How long is cardiopulmonary resuscitation after each shock?
Two minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation follow each shock.
Vasopressor repeated through every arrest rhythm?
Epinephrine, given every 3 to 5 minutes during the arrest.
Breathing rate with continuous compressions once intubated?
One breath every 6 seconds while chest compressions continue.
Antiarrhythmic for ventricular fibrillation persisting after shocks?
Amiodarone, given when fibrillation persists after shocks and epinephrine.
Drug for fibrillation still refractory after amiodarone?
Lidocaine, considered when fibrillation stays refractory after amiodarone.
Asystole on the monitor?
Rate 0 with no rhythm, P waves, PR interval or QRS complexes.
Pulseless electrical activity on the monitor?
An organized rhythm, such as sinus rhythm, but no pulse.
Two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity in adults?
Hypovolemia and hypoxia, the two leading causes in adults.
First action in asystole or pulseless electrical activity?
Start chest compressions immediately; do not shock.
Airway timing in asystole or pulseless electrical activity?
Consider intubating early while compressions continue.
Mainstays of treatment for asystole and pulseless electrical activity?
High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.
Prognosis of asystole and pulseless electrical activity?
Poor; they are usually end-of-life rhythms.
Arrest rhythms with the best prognosis?
Ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, the shockable rhythms.
Coarse versus fine ventricular fibrillation?
Large versus small chaotic waves; both are pulseless ventricular fibrillation.

name: Acute & Recurrent Pericarditis
cards: Most common disorder involving the pericardium?
Acute pericarditis.
How long does acute pericarditis last?
Less than 4 to 6 weeks.
Define incessant pericarditis.
Symptoms for more than 4 to 6 weeks, up to 3 months, without sustained remission.
Define recurrent pericarditis.
Symptoms return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer.
Define chronic pericarditis.
Symptoms persisting for more than 3 months.
Annual incidence of acute pericarditis?
About 27.7 per 100,000 people a year.
Share of nonischemic chest pain admissions that are acute pericarditis?
About 5% of emergency department admissions for nonischemic chest pain.
How often does acute pericarditis recur?
In about 15 to 30% of patients.
Most common cause of acute pericarditis?
Idiopathic, and most idiopathic cases are likely viral.
Classic viral causes of pericarditis?
Coxsackievirus and echovirus; also cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus.
Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery?
Dressler syndrome.
Blood urea nitrogen level linked to uremic pericarditis?
Above 60 mg/dL.
Drugs causing pericarditis through drug-induced lupus?
Procainamide and hydralazine.
Leading cause of acute pericarditis in an African series?
Tuberculosis, about 69.5% of cases.
Treatment of uremic pericarditis?
Dialysis.
Character of acute pericarditis chest pain?
Sharp, pleuritic substernal pain, worse supine and on inspiration.
Position that relieves pericarditis pain?
Sitting up and leaning forward.
How many diagnostic criteria make acute pericarditis?
Two of four.
The four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis?
Sharp substernal chest pain, friction rub, widespread ST elevation, new or worsening effusion.
Most specific examination finding of acute pericarditis?
The pericardial friction rub.
Classic sound of a pericardial friction rub?
Triphasic, scratchy or squeaking, loudest at the left sternal border.
How to tell a pleural rub from a pericardial rub?
A pleural rub stops when the breath is held; a pericardial rub persists.
Classic electrocardiogram of acute pericarditis?
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression.
Lead showing reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation in pericarditis?
Lead aVR.
Stage 3 of the pericarditis electrocardiogram?
The flattened T waves become inverted.
Echocardiogram in uncomplicated acute pericarditis?
Often normal unless there is a pericardial effusion.
Chest radiograph in acute pericarditis?
Typically normal.
What does a raised troponin in pericarditis suggest?
Myopericarditis: the myocardium is also involved.
Fever threshold marking high-risk pericarditis?
Above 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit).
Time without improvement that marks high-risk pericarditis?
No improvement after 7 days of anti-inflammatory plus colchicine therapy.
First-line therapy for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis?
A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine.
How long is colchicine given after a first episode?
About 3 months.
How long is colchicine given after a recurrence?
6 months or more.
Pericarditis treatment when anti-inflammatories cannot be taken?
Prednisone (with colchicine).
Pericarditis treatment after a myocardial infarction?
Aspirin plus colchicine; avoid other anti-inflammatories and glucocorticoids.
Activity restriction after acute pericarditis?
No strenuous activity for at least 1 month, heart rate under 100.
Symptom-based rule for starting the taper?
Symptom-free for at least 24 hours.
What does no response within 1 week suggest?
A cause other than idiopathic or viral pericarditis.
C-reactive protein level marking the inflammatory phenotype?
Above 10 mg/L.
Anti-interleukin-1 drugs for recurrent pericarditis?
Anakinra and rilonacept.
Recurrent or colchicine-resistant pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype: preferred therapy?
Anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept).
Second recurrence with systemic autoimmune disease: added drug?
Low-to-moderate dose prednisone.
Risk factors for multiple recurrences?
High C-reactive protein, severe late gadolinium enhancement, autoimmune cause.
Imaging recommended to risk-stratify recurrent pericarditis?
Cardiac magnetic resonance.
Share of pericarditis patients with the poorest prognosis?
About 15%, those with high-risk features.
Who should a patient with recurrent pericarditis be referred to?
Cardiology.

name: Constrictive Pericarditis & Tamponade
cards: Define constrictive pericarditis.
Fibrous scarring of the pericardium with loss of elasticity.
Define cardiac tamponade.
Pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart.
Define effusive-constrictive pericarditis.
Constriction that persists after the pericardial effusion is drained.
Most common cause of constrictive pericarditis?
Idiopathic or viral, more than 50% of cases.
Symptoms of constrictive pericarditis?
Fluid overload (edema, anasarca) and low output (fatigue, exertional dyspnea).
Kussmaul sign?
Jugular venous pressure rises on inspiration instead of falling.
Condition marked by the Kussmaul sign?
Constrictive pericarditis.
Timing of the pericardial knock?
Early diastole, slightly earlier than a third heart sound.
How specific is the pericardial knock?
Pathognomonic when present, but rare.
Echocardiogram signs of constrictive pericarditis?
Thick pericardium, septal bounce, respiratory variation in filling, biatrial enlargement.
Arrhythmia common in advanced constrictive pericarditis?
Atrial fibrillation.
Chest radiograph calcification in constrictive pericarditis?
Highly specific, but most patients have none.
Natriuretic peptide in constriction versus restriction?
Likely lower in constrictive pericarditis than restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Cardiac mimic of constrictive pericarditis?
Restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Noncardiac mimic of constrictive pericarditis?
Cirrhosis: both cause ascites and fluid overload.
Test occasionally needed to confirm constriction?
Right heart catheterization with coronary angiography.
Definitive treatment of constrictive pericarditis?
Pericardiectomy.
Diuretics before pericardiectomy?
Used sparingly in the preoperative period.
Early, stable constrictive pericarditis: first step?
A 2-to-3-month trial of anti-inflammatories, colchicine and diuretics.
Survival after pericardiectomy?
Nearly 80% at 5 years, nearly 60% at 10 years.
Cause of constriction with the worst survival?
Prior ionizing radiation.
Beck triad?
Muffled heart sounds, distended jugular veins, hypotension.
Pulsus paradoxus?
A 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration.
Hallmark examination finding of tamponade?
Pulsus paradoxus.
Electrocardiogram finding fairly specific for tamponade?
Electrical alternans: QRS height alternates beat to beat.
Echocardiogram finding of tamponade?
Right ventricular diastolic collapse.
Chest radiograph of a large effusion?
Globular water-bottle heart, clear lungs.
Catheterization finding of tamponade?
Equalization of pressures in all chambers.
Venous waveform in tamponade?
Prominent x descent, absent y descent.
How is tamponade confirmed?
By the hemodynamic and clinical response to pericardial drainage.
What does sinus tachycardia mean in tamponade?
Significant compromise: immediate pericardiocentesis is indicated.
Definitive treatment of cardiac tamponade?
Expedient pericardiocentesis.
Why give intravenous fluid in tamponade?
To raise preload and prevent right ventricular collapse until drainage.
Drug class avoided before tamponade drainage?
Diuretics, because they lower preload.
Hemorrhagic tamponade after trauma?
Emergent surgery to repair the injury.
Mimics of acute tamponade?
Right ventricular infarction, aortic dissection, massive pulmonary embolism.
Mimics of subacute tamponade?
Constrictive pericarditis, heart failure, cirrhosis.
Mechanical complication of infarction causing tamponade?
Free-wall rupture.
Long-term prognosis of tamponade depends on?
The underlying cause.

name: Pericardial Effusion
cards: Define pericardial effusion.
Extra fluid accumulating in the pericardial space around the heart.
Share of adults with a pericardial effusion (Framingham)?
Up to 6.5% of the general adult population.
Share of hospital admissions with cardiac tamponade?
About 0.05%.
Symptoms of a small effusion?
None, or vague: dull chest ache, fatigue, dyspnea.
Why does a large effusion cause hoarseness?
Recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement.
Other symptoms of a large effusion?
Dysphagia, nausea, hiccups and cough.
Volume enough for tamponade when fluid gathers fast?
Under 200 mL.
Why can a chronic effusion grow large without tamponade?
The pericardium stretches over time.
Test required to confirm a pericardial effusion?
Echocardiogram.
Echocardiogram look of a large effusion?
The heart swinging in the fluid.
Important cause of effusion and tamponade, especially in older adults?
Malignancy.
Metabolic causes of pericardial effusion?
Uremia and hypothyroidism.
Thyroid state causing a pericardial effusion?
Hypothyroidism with myxedema.
Chemotherapy drug causing pericardial effusion?
Doxorubicin.
Antihypertensive causing pericardial effusion?
Minoxidil.
Antiseizure drug causing pericardial effusion?
Phenytoin.
Infections causing pericardial effusion?
Human immunodeficiency virus, Lyme disease, coxsackievirus, tuberculosis.
Test for lupus in a young woman with an effusion?
Antinuclear antibody.
Tests for nephrotic syndrome in an effusion workup?
Albumin and urine protein.
Cancers to look for with an unexplained effusion?
Breast cancer and lung cancer.
When is diagnostic pericardiocentesis considered?
Tamponade drainage, suspected neoplastic, purulent or tuberculous disease, or unexplained moderate-to-large effusion.
Fluid study for tuberculous effusion?
Acid-fast bacilli stain and mycobacterial culture.
Fluid study for malignant effusion?
Cytology.
Pericardial fluid test rarely helpful for diagnosis?
Cell count and differential.
Fluid studies for bacterial or fungal effusion?
Gram stain and bacterial and fungal cultures.
Procedure for recurrent or loculated posterior effusions?
Pericardial window or pericardiectomy.
Main determinant of effusion prognosis?
The underlying cause.
Median survival with a symptomatic malignant effusion?
2 to 4 months.
Consult recommended for a symptomatic malignant effusion?
Palliative care.
Follow-up of every large pericardial effusion?
Serial transthoracic echocardiograms.
Specialist follow-up for a tuberculous effusion?
Infectious disease.
Older adults: why use anti-inflammatories cautiously?
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are on the Beers list.
Older adults: colchicine adjustment?
Consider a dose reduction.
Older adults: corticosteroid concern?
Increased osteoporosis risk.
Older adults: surgical risk?
Higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions.
Older adults: need after prolonged illness?
Rehabilitation.

name: Endocarditis: Sites, Signs & Organisms
cards: Most common site of infective endocarditis?
The heart valves.
Which side of a ventricular septal defect gets infected?
The low-pressure side, which is the right side.
What damages non-valve endocardium enough to be infected?
Aberrant jets of blood or foreign bodies.
What makes up an infective vegetation?
Platelets, fibrin, micro-colonies of organisms and inflammatory cells.
When to suspect health care-associated endocarditis?
A hospitalized patient with fevers and positive blood cultures without an apparent source.
Share of cases in patients over 60?
More than 50%.
Which sex gets infective endocarditis more often?
Men.
Share of native valve endocarditis that is health care-associated?
About 25-35%.
When is prosthetic valve endocarditis risk greatest?
Within the first year after valve replacement.
How soon can pacemaker or defibrillator endocarditis occur?
Within weeks of implantation or of a generator change.
Leading predisposing conditions in high-income countries?
Degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices.
Can endocarditis occur in younger people?
Yes: risk is highest in the elderly, but it can occur at any age.
Tempo of acute infective endocarditis?
Rapid onset over 3-10 days with high fevers and systemic toxicity.
Tempo of subacute infective endocarditis?
Lower fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks to months.
Which form seeds extracardiac sites?
Acute infective endocarditis; subacute disease rarely metastasizes.
Untreated acute endocarditis progresses to death within?
Weeks.
What interrupts the gradual course of subacute endocarditis?
A major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm.
Most common symptom of infective endocarditis?
Fever.
Symptom linked to people who inject drugs?
Cough (the lung is a listed embolic site).
Roth spots?
White-centered retinal hemorrhages from vasculitis of small retinal arteries.
Splinter hemorrhages?
Thin lines under the fingernails and toenails, an embolic phenomenon.
Where do endocarditis petechiae appear?
Palate (buccal mucosa), conjunctiva and skin of the extremities.
Osler nodes?
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads; immunologic; fade in 2-3 days.
Janeway lesions?
Painless flat hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles; vascular (embolic).
Which peripheral sign is associated with acute endocarditis?
Janeway lesions.
Cause of a new murmur in endocarditis?
Valve damage or rupture of the chordae tendineae, producing regurgitation.
Cause of heart failure in endocarditis?
Valvular dysfunction.
Perivalvular abscess extending into the epicardium causes?
Pericarditis.
Perivalvular abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum causes?
Interruption of the conduction system.
Classic organisms of acute endocarditis?
Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci.
Classic organism of subacute endocarditis?
Viridans streptococci.
Oral cavity source points to?
Viridans streptococci.
Skin source points to?
Staphylococci.
Upper respiratory tract source points to?
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group.
Gastrointestinal source points to?
Streptococcus gallolyticus.
Genitourinary source points to?
Enterococci.
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis organisms?
Coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus.
Late prosthetic valve endocarditis organism?
Viridans streptococci.
Gram stain of the HACEK organisms?
Gram-negative (fastidious gram-negative coccobacilli).
Organism of fungal endocarditis?
Candida (and Aspergillus).
Main organism in people who inject drugs?
Staphylococcus aureus: over 60% overall, 80-90% of tricuspid cases.
Largest share of health care-associated native valve endocarditis?
Staphylococcus aureus, about 52%.
Largest share of device endocarditis?
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, about 41%.

name: Endocarditis: Duke Criteria & Work-up
icon: <rect x="5" y="4" width="14" height="17" rx="2"/><path d="M9 4V3h6v1"/><path d="M9 13l2 2 4-4"/>
cards: Major criterion 1?
A positive blood culture: typical organism in two separate cultures, or persistently positive.
Typical organisms for the culture criterion?
Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus, HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), Staphylococcus aureus, community enterococci without a focus.
Persistently positive cultures are drawn how far apart?
More than 12 hours apart.
Major criterion 2?
Endocardial involvement: positive echocardiogram or new valvular regurgitation.
Echocardiogram findings that meet the major criterion?
Oscillating intracardiac mass, abscess, or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve.
Does a louder preexisting murmur meet the major criterion?
No; an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is not sufficient.
Minor criterion: predisposition?
A predisposing heart condition or injection drug use.
Minor criterion: fever?
38.0 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or more.
Duke category of Janeway lesions?
Vascular phenomenon.
Duke category of conjunctival hemorrhages?
Vascular phenomenon.
Duke category of Osler nodes?
Immunologic phenomenon.
Duke category of Roth spots?
Immunologic phenomenon.
Duke category of glomerulonephritis?
Immunologic phenomenon.
Duke category of a septic pulmonary infarct?
Vascular phenomenon.
Single positive cultures excluded as contaminants?
Coagulase-negative staphylococci and diphtheroids.
Definite endocarditis needs?
Two major, or one major and three minor, or five minor criteria.
Possible endocarditis needs?
One major and one minor, or three minor criteria.
Two major criteria and no minor criteria?
Definite endocarditis.
Duke category of rheumatoid factor?
Immunologic phenomenon.
When is a transesophageal study required for optimal assessment?
Possible prosthetic valve endocarditis, or complicated endocarditis.
How many blood culture sets, and from where?
Three sets, from separate sites, within 24 hours.
Cultures when the presentation suggests acute endocarditis?
Two cultures within the first 1-2 hours, then empiric antibiotics.
Cultures or antibiotics first?
Cultures first; empiric antibiotics start only after cultures are drawn.
Most sensitive and specific imaging for endocarditis?
Transesophageal echocardiogram; it also defines the extent of disease.
Does a normal transesophageal echocardiogram rule endocarditis out?
No, not necessarily.
Complete blood count in endocarditis?
Leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume.
Urinalysis in endocarditis?
Hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
Mimic: non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis?
Systemic lupus erythematosus.
Mimic: thromboemboli plus cardiac valve disease?
Antiphospholipid syndrome.
Mimic: myalgia with raised inflammatory markers?
Polymyalgia rheumatica.
Mimic: fever and a new murmur with a tumor plop?
Atrial myxoma.

name: Endocarditis: Treatment & Prophylaxis
icon: <rect x="3" y="9" width="18" height="6" rx="3" transform="rotate(-35 12 12)"/><path d="M10 8.5l4 7"/>
cards: What must antibiotic therapy for endocarditis be?
Bactericidal, prolonged and parenteral; every organism in the vegetation must be killed.
Course length, counted from when?
Typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative blood culture.
Empiric therapy must cover?
Staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci.
Empiric regimen: native valve or subacute presentation?
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.
Empiric regimen: prosthetic valve more than 1 year old?
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.
Empiric regimen: prosthetic valve 1 year old or less?
Vancomycin plus gentamicin plus cefepime.
Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, native valve?
Nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, native valve?
Vancomycin or daptomycin.
Added for Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve?
Rifampin and gentamicin.
Viridans streptococci?
Penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin; or vancomycin.
When is the 2-week gentamicin regimen allowed?
Uncomplicated, rapid response to therapy and no chronic kidney disease.
Enterococci?
Ampicillin (or penicillin G) plus gentamicin.
HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms?
Ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam.
Consultant for antibiotics and outpatient monitoring?
Infectious disease.
Consultant for surgery and anticoagulation needs?
Cardiothoracic surgery.
Consultant for harm reduction?
Addiction medicine, for people who inject drugs.
Most common indication for surgery?
Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction.
Why is fungal endocarditis a surgical indication?
It is difficult to cure with medication alone.
Anticoagulation in native valve endocarditis?
Not beneficial.
Anticoagulation with a prosthetic valve?
Controversial.
Most lethal endocarditis organism?
Staphylococcus aureus, deadliest on prosthetic valves (about 50%).
Prognosis of viridans streptococcal endocarditis?
Relatively good if antibiotics start before complications occur.
Why is enterococcal endocarditis hard to treat?
Antibiotic resistance; valve replacement is needed in about 30-40%.
Most likely complication of fungal endocarditis?
Embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries.
Prophylaxis: which dental procedures?
Those that manipulate the gums or periapical region or perforate the oral mucosa.
Prophylaxis: which respiratory procedures?
Those that incise or biopsy the mucosa, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy.
Prophylaxis for bronchoscopy?
Not unless it involves incision of the mucosa, such as a biopsy.
Prophylaxis for colonoscopy, upper endoscopy or cystoscopy?
Not recommended in the absence of active infection.
Prophylaxis for bleeding from lip trauma?
Not required.
Standard prophylaxis regimen?
A single dose of oral amoxicillin, 30-60 minutes before the procedure.
Prophylaxis: no penicillin allergy, cannot take oral?
Ampicillin intramuscular or intravenous (or cefazolin or ceftriaxone).
Prophylaxis: penicillin allergy, can take oral?
Azithromycin or clarithromycin, doxycycline, or cephalexin.
Prophylaxis: penicillin allergy, cannot take oral?
Cefazolin or ceftriaxone, intramuscular or intravenous.
Why was clindamycin dropped from prophylaxis?
Risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
Cephalosporins are avoided after which penicillin reactions?
Anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.
High-risk condition: prior infection?
Previous infective endocarditis.
High-risk period after congenital heart repair with prosthetic material?
The first 6 months.
Pediatric endocarditis is driven by?
Congenital heart disease and indwelling central venous catheters.
Infant presentation of endocarditis?
Nonspecific, sepsis-like illness: poor feeding, respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension.
Most common organism, child over 1 year with congenital disease?
Viridans group streptococci; Staphylococcus aureus next.
Shunt infection sign in cyanotic congenital heart disease?
Falling oxygen saturation; the murmur may not change.
